name: Luri
description: Luri, also written Lori, encompasses related Southwestern Iranian varieties spoken across the Zagros Mountains of western and southwestern Iran. Its regional diversity and connections with Persian and Kurdish make it important to distinguish linguistic classification from community identity. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Luri: Languages and Communities of the Zagros | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Luri's regional varieties, Southwestern Iranian relationships, and the distinction between language and community identity.

content.heading: A language landscape across the Zagros
content.content:
Luri is best approached as a group of related regional varieties rather than a single uniform way of speaking. Also spelled Lori in linguistic scholarship, it belongs to the Southwestern branch of Iranian languages, alongside Persian. Here, “Iranian” names a linguistic family; it does not mean that every member is a form of the national language. Luri-speaking areas extend through the Zagros, including Lorestan, Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari, Kohgiluyeh and Boyer-Ahmad, and parts of neighboring provinces. Colin MacKinnon's account describes speakers in both settled and migratory communities. [s1]

Regional names matter. Khorramabadi, associated with Khorramabad in Lorestan, is one Northern Luri variety. Bakhtiari and Mamasani belong to the southern grouping in MacKinnon's description. This classification is useful for orientation, but readers should identify the particular variety behind a recording, dictionary, or grammatical example rather than assuming that it represents all Luri speech. [s1]

content.heading: Related speech, distinct identities
content.content:
Different scholarly groupings emphasize different aspects of this diversity. Erik Anonby's sociolinguistic account distinguishes Northern Luri, Bakhtiari, and Southern Luri, while MacKinnon places Bakhtiari within a broader southern division. The labels therefore need to be read with the author's definitions in view. [s1][s2]

Anonby describes a continuum connecting neighboring Kurdish and Southwestern Iranian varieties. A continuum does not imply that speakers at opposite ends readily understand one another: his account reports substantial intelligibility barriers between major Luri varieties. Linguistic similarity also does not determine ethnic identity. Bakhtiari speakers may emphasize their Bakhtiari affiliation, while some communities identifying as Lur speak another language. In transitional areas, community identity alone is consequently an unreliable guide to linguistic classification. [s2]

For an international reader, the practical lesson is to keep three questions separate: what people call themselves, what they call their speech, and how researchers classify that speech. These can overlap without producing identical boundaries. [s2]

content.heading: Why local documentation matters
content.content:
A research project presented by The Iranian Highlands in 2023 identifies reliable, comprehensive descriptions of many Luri dialects as an outstanding need. Its proposed documentation focuses on Bahma'i around Likak, Mamasani around Nurabad, and Rumeshkani around Cheghabal. The project connects local documentation with historical questions about Luri's relationships to Persian, other Southwestern Iranian varieties, and its northern neighbors. These are research objectives, rather than evidence that all the proposed work has been completed. [s3]

This emphasis on particular communities offers a useful way to explore Luri: begin with a named locality and variety, then place it within the wider Zagros landscape. It preserves distinctions that a single language label can conceal and leaves room for historical relationships still being investigated. [s3]

name: Gilaki
description: Gilaki is a Northwestern Iranian language of the Caspian subgroup, associated with Gilan in northern Iran. Its eastern and western varieties and distinctive grammatical structures show why it should be understood as a language with internal diversity rather than simply a regional Persian accent. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Gilaki: Gilan's Caspian Language | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Gilaki's eastern and western varieties, its place among Caspian languages, and the grammar that distinguishes it from Persian.

content.heading: Gilaki within a multilingual province
content.content:
Gilaki belongs to the Caspian subgroup of Northwestern Iranian. Its association with Gilan, on Iran's southern Caspian coast, should not turn the province into an imagined single-language territory. Donald Stilo's survey also identifies Talyshi, Rudbari, Tati, Kurdish, and non-Iranian languages in Gilan. A provincial name is therefore a geographic starting point, rather than a complete description of the language used by every resident. [s1]

Stilo distinguishes eastern and western Gilaki, with the Sefidrud River serving as their general dividing line. Toward Mazandaran, the picture becomes more complicated: transitional varieties around Tonekabon and Kelardasht do not fit neatly into a simple Gilaki–Mazandarani division. His account argues that their limited mutual intelligibility with either language merits treating them separately. This is a scholarly classification proposal, rather than a reason to erase speakers' own local labels. [s1]

content.heading: A different way to build a phrase
content.content:
Grammar provides a concrete route beyond the idea of Gilaki as accented Persian. Mansour Shabani and Sahar Taghipour's study examines the Eshkevarat variety, rather than claiming to describe every Gilaki dialect. Its published abstract reports that noun phrases and most adpositional phrases are head-final: the central word follows material that depends on it. [s2]

The study also describes a linking element called “Reverse Ezafe.” An ezafe is a grammatical connector within a phrase. In the construction discussed here, certain modifiers or the complement of a postposition are linked to a following head. A postposition performs a role comparable to an English preposition but follows its complement. The authors distinguish the properties of this linker in possessive and adpositional constructions from its behavior with attributive adjectives. These findings show that even a small connecting element can reveal substantial internal organization. [s2]

The important qualification is local scope. A description of Eshkevarat supplies evidence about that variety; extending every detail to Rasht, Lahijan, or another community would require additional evidence. Readers comparing learning materials should therefore look for the locality represented as well as the name Gilaki. [s2]

content.heading: Contact without linguistic sameness
content.content:
Stilo documents extensive Persian influence on Gilaki while also identifying grammatical contrasts and retained vocabulary. Borrowing and structural change do not, by themselves, make the languages identical. His survey also records Gilaki literary and newspaper activity, although its publication history means it cannot establish the extent of such activity today. [s1]

The most useful introduction to Gilaki therefore combines a regional map with a local grammatical description. The map explains variation; the grammar shows how speakers organize meaning. Together, they offer a more precise account than either a provincial stereotype or a claim that all Caspian speech is interchangeable. [s1][s2]

name: Mazandarani
description: Mazandarani, also called Tabari, is a Northwestern Iranian language associated with the southern Caspian region. Research on local speech and nineteenth-century texts reveals both regional diversity and historical continuity, alongside changes linked to contact with Persian. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Mazandarani: Tabari Speech and Written Evidence | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Mazandarani through its Caspian setting, local varieties, Persian contact, and documented nineteenth-century texts.

content.heading: A Caspian language with local varieties
content.content:
Mazandarani is also known as Tabari; Habib Borjian's work on historical texts uses the term New Tabari as well. It is a Northwestern Iranian language associated with Mazandaran, south of the Caspian Sea. The alternative names matter when searching catalogs: material relevant to the same language may be indexed under different headings. [s1][s2]

The language's geography should not be reduced to an administrative outline. Borjian's typological survey distinguishes a central area across the coastal plains from peripheral varieties toward the east, west, and southern highlands. It describes variation both between river valleys and between lowland and highland communities. Local dialects consequently belong within the account, rather than appearing as exceptions to a supposedly uniform provincial language. [s1]

content.heading: What a village study can reveal
content.content:
Kalijan Rostaq, a rural district in the Caspian forest south of Sari, provides a focused example. In the abstract of his study, Borjian describes neighboring villages sharing a local Mazandarani dialect. He reports phonological, morphological, and vocabulary features that have been lost in the urban Sari variety through contact with Persian. Phonology concerns a language's sound system; morphology concerns the forms and internal structure of words. [s3]

This comparison is valuable because language change can affect several parts of speech at once. It also needs careful interpretation. Evidence from one district does not establish that every village preserves the same features or that all city speakers use an identical variety. Borjian's broader survey likewise treats Mazandarani as internally varied and does not identify one dialect as the standard or formal variety. [s1][s3]

The Kalijan Rostaq study's abstract also identifies cultural vocabulary in its glossary as becoming obsolete. Such documentation connects linguistic description with local knowledge: losing an expression can make older accounts of work, objects, or practices harder to interpret. The abstract establishes this concern, but does not justify a quantified claim about language loss across the province. [s3]

content.heading: Written evidence of continuity and change
content.content:
Written documents offer another perspective. Borjian's article on two Mazandarani texts examines material written in Barforush in 1889 and subsequently published in facsimile by Jacques de Morgan. According to the article's abstract, the study provides transcription, translation, and a glossary. It finds substantial continuity with later Mazandarani while also identifying vocabulary and grammatical features no longer in use. [s2]

That combination is more informative than calling the language either unchanged or wholly transformed. Historical texts preserve forms that modern speakers may not recognize, while still recording a related linguistic system. They can also preserve descriptions of events, giving language documentation a role in historical research. The inspected abstract supports these general findings; it does not provide access to the detailed textual readings. [s2]

Mazandarani is therefore best explored through connected kinds of evidence: local speech, comparisons across the Caspian landscape, and dated documents. Each answers a different question, and none alone supplies a current count of fluent speakers. [s1][s2][s3]
